Case Study — Project 01

Solar Panel Model

2024 Algoma Regional Science Fair · Grade 10 · Team Project
🏆 1st Place, Intermediate Division + Computer Science & Computer Engineering Awards

Overview

For the 2024 Algoma Regional Science Fair, our team set out to build a working model of a dual-axis solar tracker — a small-scale solar panel that could automatically reposition itself to follow the sun's movement across the sky, maximizing the energy it captured over the course of a day.

It was our team's first time working with Arduino, and the project ended up being as much a lesson in troubleshooting hardware under pressure as it was in solar energy.

Objectives

  • Design a solar panel model that automatically tracks the sun's position across all axes to maximize energy capture efficiency
  • Learn to program and wire an Arduino-based control system from scratch, with no prior experience
  • Build a stable, durable physical structure that could reliably support the moving panel assembly through repeated testing

Process

01

Building the control system

Used an Arduino microcontroller as the "brain" of the tracker, paired with photoresistive light sensors positioned to detect which direction held the strongest light source. The Arduino compared readings across the sensors and adjusted the panel's position to follow the light.

02

Challenge — fragile connections

Early in testing, the wiring between the photoresistors and the Arduino kept coming loose and breaking the circuit. Resolved this by soldering the connections directly and wrapping them in electrical tape, creating a joint durable enough to survive repeated handling and testing.

03

Challenge — stability & weight

The moving head of the model, which housed the panel and sensors, made the frame unstable and prone to tipping at steeper angles. Researched several 3D-printable base designs and adapted one to give the frame a wider, more stable footing that allowed free movement on all axes without tipping — and swapped the original heavy styrofoam body for lighter, easier-to-modify cardboard.

04

Testing & iteration

Ran repeated rounds of testing and adjustment rather than assuming the first fix would hold, refining both the wiring and the frame until the tracker moved smoothly and reliably followed a light source through a full range of motion.

Outcomes

✓
1st Place, Intermediate Division
✓

✓

This project became the foundation for how I approach hands-on engineering problems: test the material or the wiring, don't just assume the first attempt will hold.
